worksheet.title: Do They Meet?
worksheet.subtitle: Same number means they meet
worksheet.learning_goal: I can run two scripts at the same time and tell if the sprites land on the same number.

parts.title: Meeting on the path
parts.text: Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) both start on the green flag ▶ and run at the SAME time. If they land on the SAME number, they MEET. If they land on different numbers, they do not. Read each script, find where each lands, then check: do they meet?

parts.title: Where does Bit land?
parts.prompt: Read Bit's script from 1: forward 2, then back 1. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: Where does Pixel land?
parts.prompt: Read Pixel's script from 4: back 1, then back 1. What number does Pixel land on?

parts.title: Do they meet?
parts.prompt: The green flag starts BOTH scripts at once. Write where each lands. Bit: ____  Pixel: ____. Do they land on the SAME number? Circle YES or NO.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Two scripts run at the same time. To tell if the sprites MEET, find where each one lands and check if the two numbers are the same. Same number = they meet.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students run two concurrent scripts and decide a combined result: do the two sprites land on the SAME number (meet) or not? Judging 'meet / don't meet' depends on holding BOTH parallel landings in mind at once — the Grade-2 C3.2 reasoning about how concurrent code behaves together. Here the scripts were written so the sprites DO meet (both land on 2).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 2 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: two counters (green for Bit, purple for Pixel) on a floor number path 0-5; after 'green flag!', see whether both counters end on the same square.

parts.title: Run it (about 20 min)
text: 1. I DO: read Bit's script — 'start 1, forward 2 → 3, back 1 → 2.' Bit lands on 2.
2. WE DO: read Pixel's script — 'start 4, back 1 → 3, back 1 → 2.' Press the green flag so BOTH run together.
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — students see both land on 2, so they circle YES, they meet.
4. Connect: 'They started in different places but both scripts ended on the same number — so they meet.'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — Bit: 1 → forward 2 → 3 → back 1 → 2. Bit lands on 2.
Ex 2 — Pixel: 4 → back 1 → 3 → back 1 → 2. Pixel lands on 2.
Ex 3 — both start on the green flag and both land on 2 → SAME number → YES, they MEET.
Interaction note: the scripts run independently and at the same time; we compare the two final positions to decide if they meet.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common error: assuming sprites that start in different places can never meet — they can, if their scripts bring them to the same number.
Common error: running one script, then the other, as if sequential — the green flag starts BOTH at once (concurrent).
Simplify: find each landing first, then just ask 'are these two numbers the same?'
Extend: ask students to change ONE move in Pixel's script so the sprites would NOT meet.
Success indicator: the child lands both on 2 and circles YES, explaining the two scripts ended on the same number.
